title: Tuesday, November 3: Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen, and two more
description:
The three biggest Hacker News stories for Tuesday, November 3.

1. Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen
   Article: https://rikiyat.github.io/blog/weight-space-programming/
   Discussion: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50341174

2. WTF Ubuntu?
   Article: https://chalmovsky.com/posts/wtf-ubuntu
   Discussion: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50337608

3. Show HN: Subvocal – Talk to your computer without making noise
   Discussion: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50340088

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: This is Upvoted, the top of Hacker News for Tuesday, November 3. I'm Maya.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: And I'm Theo. Big one today: an AI model that reads neural network weights like it's reading code.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Then a critical Linux bug that Debian fixed weeks ago, and Ubuntu still hasn't.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: And glasses that let you talk to your computer without making a sound.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Let's get into it.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Okay, so the top story, with about twenty-nine hundred points, is a blog post called Weight-Space Programming. The claim is that GPT-6 Astra can look at the raw weights of a neural network and work out what it does.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Just the numbers? No running it?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Just the numbers. They handed it about seventeen thousand weights from a tiny network trained to play a video game, no tools, and it said Breakout, ninety-nine percent confident.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Huh. Okay, that's a fun party trick, but—

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: But wait, it gets bigger. They asked it to make Qwen three point five, a small open model, better at math. No training at all.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: So what did it actually change?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It noticed the model kept getting stuck in reasoning loops. Eighty-five of its first ninety-six practice answers just ran until they hit the length limit. Astra traced that to one direction in two of its layers and subtracted it out.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Like finding the one stuck key on a keyboard and popping it off.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Pretty much. It touched a tiny fraction of a percent of the weights, and the math benchmark went from about eight percent to forty-eight.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Right, and that's exactly where the thread pumps the brakes. One commenter who says they do research in weight-space learning basically begged people to read the paper before losing their minds. Their take is that the write-up oversells it.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Because Qwen already knew the math?

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: That's the argument, yeah. It wasn't taught anything new, it was un-stuck. And a few people pointed out that removing a direction that causes looping was already a known technique.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Someone also brought receipts on how old this field is. Predicting and generating weights goes back years. One person said their master's thesis in twenty eighteen was on it.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: And not everyone could reproduce it. Somebody tried the same trick on a small model that turns plain English into shell commands. It fixed some mistakes and broke others. No net gain.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Though on the other side, one commenter ran the same prompts on a Qwen model on their own laptop, and it got Pac-Man, Breakout and Pong. It only missed Freeway.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Which, to be fair, I'd miss too.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So where it lands: maybe not magic, but a lot of people upvoted just because they hadn't realized this was possible at all.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: And they want to see where it goes as the models get bigger. Fair enough.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Story two has a title I'll paraphrase as: what on earth, Ubuntu? It's about a Linux kernel bug, rated nine point eight out of ten on the CVSS scale.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's about as bad as it goes, right?

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Close to it. It's in the kernel's networking code, it's been there since twenty sixteen, and it can be hit remotely. Anthropic says it built a working exploit that gets root on a server.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Oof. So everyone just patches, right?

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Debian shipped a fix on October sixteenth. The author says that, more than two weeks later, every supported Ubuntu release was still listed as vulnerable. LTS included.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Wait, really?

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Really. And they're angry about it. They point out that volunteer distros shipped the fix while Canonical, which sells security subscriptions, hadn't. They took their Ubuntu servers offline and say they're moving off for good.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Okay, but I want the other side. Is it actually as dangerous as nine point eight sounds?

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: That's a real debate in the thread. One commenter noted the predicted chance of exploitation is under one percent, and that most advisories describe a crash, not a takeover. Anthropic is the main source for the root exploit.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Huh. So it's partly a communications problem.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: That's how a few people put it. Ubuntu's own page labels it high priority, not critical, and the link explaining why is, well, almost empty.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Did Canonical say anything?

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Someone from Canonical's product team showed up. They said fixes for twenty-two oh four and newer are in the proposed pocket, being tested for stability, and they've published a blog post with details.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And the replies were, let me guess—

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Three weeks is plenty of time. Yep.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: To be fair, someone else warned that one of those proposed kernels has serious regressions. So rushing has its own cost.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Right. And one commenter thought the post itself was more outrage than detail. But others said a company charging for security gets held to a higher bar.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Last one, and it's a Show H N. Two founders, Aarush and Arnav, built smart glasses that let you talk to your computer silently. You just mouth the words.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Mouth them. Like, no sound at all?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: No sound. The glasses send out radio waves, sort of like Bluetooth, that pass through your face. Your tongue and lips change the signal, and their models decode that into text.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Okay, that's either brilliant or terrifying.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Maybe both! The origin story's great, though. They were computer science students at Georgia Tech, and at a hackathon they tried it with electrodes stuck on one founder's face.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Which I'm guessing didn't ship.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Nope. Sweat, interference, and, their words, nobody wants electrodes on their face. So they switched to radio, and they got it working across different people by paying folks to sit in booths and read prompts while wearing the glasses.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: I'll be the skeptic. Do people even talk faster than they type? One commenter said they read aloud slower than they think.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The founder answered that: most people type forty to fifty words a minute, and talk at a hundred twenty to two hundred.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Fair. What about privacy, though? Something reading your mouth all day.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That came up a lot. Some people said they'd only use it if it ran fully offline. Right now, the founder said, decoding happens in a companion app, in the cloud.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: And the accessibility angle seemed huge. One person scheduled for carpal tunnel surgery on both hands said it's exactly what they've been looking for.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And someone pointed out it could help people with tracheostomies, who can move their mouths but can't use their voice.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Plus my favorite request: please keep adjustable nose pads, from a commenter who says they have a big nose.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And the founder said yes! They're aiming to ship in the first quarter of twenty twenty-seven.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: That's Upvoted for today. Weights you can read, a patch that's late, and glasses you can whisper to without whispering.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Links to everything are in the show notes. Thanks for listening, and we'll be back tomorrow with the top of Hacker News.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: See you then.
